title: UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response
description: The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our
body: The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution".Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists."And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians."He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious group from certain areas".Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements".He said this position, which is in line with a 2024 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank.As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said.The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK."The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added.Later on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution".Announcing the closure of the consulate - which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza - Israel's Foreign Minister Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain. "Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions."He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity". The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden.It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements. The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".Elsewhere, he said the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, carried "terrible echoes of the centuries of persecution of the Jewish people" and stressed Israel had "the right to protect its people and defend its territory".However, he added, "that cannot justify what has happened in Gaza".He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes."What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry."The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this."He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law.Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK.He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel.He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel."But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews".The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests".In an interview with Jewish News, external after speaking in the Commons, Miliband said "any person who targets British Jews because of the actions of the Israeli government is an antisemite in my view", a position which he said was "shared across the House of Commons". He said the response from the Israeli government had been "deeply regrettable". Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work".He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that".Israel's foreign minister Saar said on Tuesday evening he had spoken with Tugendhat and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, thanking them "for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour government's announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office".He also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated.Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation."Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution".US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did".Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses".He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level.The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group.New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran.The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

schema.headline: UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response

title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods
description: The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on America
body: The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said that Canada is "discriminating" against the United States and outlined the import ban, to begin 29 September.Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that  his country's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.The BBC has contacted the office of the Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, for comment.The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The sides have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other.The US is Canada's largest trading partner - generally more than two-thirds of its total exports go to its neighbour.On the other hand, Canada is the US' second-largest trading partner, after Mexico, although its exports are far more diversified.Business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall.Last month, the White House had imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down.Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as sporting and fishing equipment businesses.Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday.Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting the distribution of US goods while not doing the same to such products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday.The response targets various alcoholic drinks and dairy products like whey, according to a series of White House statements signed by the president.On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moves manufacturing there.Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging tariffs scheme has upset many of the States' traditional allies.Tension between the US and Canada have now also expanded beyond tariffs. In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some Americans.

schema.headline: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods

title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity MSF warns
description: Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country,
body: Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year."War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan."MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment."After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year. In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain -  as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children."If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

schema.headline: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity MSF warns

title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
description: The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Isla
body: The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would  sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.Reacting to the news, Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill insisted that there could be "no doubt" about the British government's commitment to the Falkland Islanders.Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, McNeill said that "the decision by the Falkland Islands government to pursue hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for them to take alongside the commercial companies involved".She added that "the future of the Falkland Islands is for Falkland Islanders to determine".The simmering dispute between Britain and Argentina over the Falklands heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands.Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering".Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives. Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028.The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities."The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted. Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands.

schema.headline: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands

title: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
description: Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how i
body: Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable.Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment. But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress. The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

schema.headline: Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades

title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
description: Image caption, Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West BankByYolande KnellMiddle East corresp
body: Image caption, Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West BankByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentJuicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods."As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."Image caption, Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan ValleyWest Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories"."I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."Image caption, The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West BankMedjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley."These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank. Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs. Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth."Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says. "They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."Image caption, Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortageIsraeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.Image caption, Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summerThere have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned."A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says."I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."Image caption, Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growthIsrael's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October.He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip."The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned.Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

schema.headline: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers

title: Eiffel Tower: Investigation after female staff replaced by men for religious visit
description: An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religiou
body: An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group.A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday."Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage.BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate". Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable".An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again".In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present"."Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said.Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women".BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in a Parisian suburb.In a statement on X, BAPS said the trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation.BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.Politicians in France have condemned Saturday's incident.Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

schema.headline: Eiffel Tower: Investigation after female staff replaced by men for religious visit

title: New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani
description: Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twi
body: Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twin Towers collapsed.Speaking alongside Mamdani at Tuesday's news conference, TV host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart said the new files show the city knew by October 2001 - a month after the terrorist attacks - that the air in Manhattan was toxic."So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically.The records show asbestos was found near Ground Zero for months after the attacks at the same time people were being advised it was safe to go there.The files, which include air-quality reports and communications among city officials, include October 2001 correspondence known as the "Harding Memo". In it, an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks.The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)".City officials also told citizens to clean up dust and debris with "wet mops and rags" despite the presence of asbestos, which is only supposed to be cleaned by licensed professionals, according to another memo documenting the concerns of congressman Jerry Nadler.

schema.headline: New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani

title: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster
description: Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel.In Novemb
body: Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel.In November 2021, at least 30 men, women and children drowned when their motorised dinghy deflated and started taking on water halfway between France and the UK.The 14 defendants – mainly Afghan nationals – are accused of manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.Most of them deny the charges. Two of the 14, who are alleged to be leaders of the operation, remain on the run and are being tried in absentia.The boat left the French coast on the evening of 23 November 2021, but ran into difficulty in the middle of the Channel. One by one the occupants entered the water to try to lessen the weight, but succumbed to the cold and drowned. Only two men survived.According to the charge sheet, the defendants helped to launch "a small boat of poor quality, unfit to navigate at sea, overloaded and equipped with inadequate life-jackets".Twenty-seven bodies were found after the boat sank, and another four were confirmed missing.Many of the people who died were Iraqi Kurds, but others came from Somalia, Ethiopia, Egypt and Afghanistan. The youngest named victim was seven years old.

schema.headline: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster

title: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
description: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoi
body: Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

schema.headline: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist

title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
description: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brex
body: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.The threat of deportation came after Swedish authorities said they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily."This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden."I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government would "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear."I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said."Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation. However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.Swedish Minister for Migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously"."The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said."We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.Håkan Svenneling, Thomas's MP from the opposition Vänsterpartiet (The Left Party), has criticised the government's "inhumane migration policy". "That is why I hope that Sunday's election in Sweden will be a turning point where the opposition can form a government and change migration policy so that Joyce and other Britons with strong ties to Sweden can stay here," he told the BBC.A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

schema.headline: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years

title: Tukaram Mundhe: Maharashtra food safety officer who is a social media star
description: The images are hard to ignore.Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food coun
body: The images are hard to ignore.Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products."These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC. The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it."I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions."When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said. "Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public. The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons."While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone. "Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety."We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post."The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban."We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

schema.headline: Tukaram Mundhe: Maharashtra food safety officer who is a social media star

title: Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv
description: A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President
body: A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.Zelensky said the daytime attack was a "new page in Russian degradation", while photos shared by the president showed a partially collapsed building.At least five people have been killed in overnight and daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv. A separate attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee, officials have said.Both countries had earlier agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.Referring to Tuesday's Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian TV channel We Are Ukraine, Zelensky said: "Today, Russia carried out a strike on the media, journalists."Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts," he added in a renewed plea to Ukraine's allies in Europe, the US and around the world.We Are Ukraine has published footage which it says shows the moment the drone hit its newsroom."The footage confirms that this was not an accidental strike, but a deliberate attack targeting journalists," the channel said in a post on Telegram.A BBC team later visited the site, confirming that the TV channel's newsroom was damaged in the strike, which reportedly interrupted the live broadcast.Earlier on Tuesday, air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces carried out missile and drone strikes on Kyiv, the local authorities said.A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed three people and injured another 25, the state emergencies service DSNS said. Residential buildings were hit, including a five-storey house in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district.People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war. By Tuesday afternoon, the death toll had reached five people.According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said early on Tuesday.The talks with Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv ended without any major breakthroughs. On Tuesday evening, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a "constructive and very frank" talks on the phone, Moscow said.The two leaders spoke for an hour, Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said.The Trump administration has not publicly commented, while Witkoff earlier had said that "substantive progress was made", without giving any further details.Ushakov had said on Saturday that Trump's envoys were informed in Moscow about "the significant advances made by the Russian armed forces" on the battlefield and stressed that the Kremlin's "set objectives would be achieved".Meanwhile, Zelensky said he expected the war to continue into the winter after meeting Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv on Sunday - their first ever visit to Ukraine.Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.Putin has so far showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.

schema.headline: Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv

title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
description: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetim
body: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer."Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples."It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade."With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here."I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

schema.headline: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant

title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
description: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal ac
body: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center."After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial."My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said."Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about."I want to concentrate on the memories," he said.  "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died."They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."Image source, FBIImage caption, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted websiteMohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case."Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding dayJohn Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacksRelatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice."If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions."My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are.  I just want them convicted," he said.Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal."It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.Image source, Brett EaglesonImage caption, Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there."My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event"."I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in"."If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo."It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

schema.headline: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
